I am very happy to have been given the opportunity to write a foreword to this collection of essays in honour of my friend Professor Raymond Klibansky. I have known Professor Klibansky since the nineteen thirties when he came to Oxford as an exile from Nazi Germany. He had been bred in the great classical tradition of German scholarship and impressed very many of us, including those who had themselves enjoyed a classical education, with the breadth of his learning, his critical acumen, the readiness of his memory and his extraordinary gift for languages, both ancient and modern. He excelled us particularly in his knowledge and understanding of mediaeval philosophy which is insufficiently studied in England, where the history of philosophy is still too often taught as if Francis Bacon, Hobbes and Descartes were born in the century in which Aristotle died.

In those early days at Oxford, Professor Klibansky was occupied more with research than teaching, but in his long tenure of a Professorship at McGill, where he went soon after the war, during which he displayed an uncommon gift for the subtleties of Political Intelligence, he has succeeded in communicating to his many pupils both his enthusiasm for ideas and some measure of his own high standard of scholarship. This standard is revealed in his work on the Corpus Platonicum and in his numerous critical editions of important philosophical texts. A lover of libraries, he enjoys the gift of serendipity, and the knowledge to appreciate the historical value of his discoveries.

Though he can be impatient of poor scholarship or the pretentious verbiage, which sometimes passes for philosophical profundity, Professor Klibansky’s philosophical sympathies are wide. He has been keenly alive to the importance of promoting international understanding among philosophers and has devoted much time and energy to this cause. A former President of the International Institute of Philosophy, he has for many years borne the chief responsibility for the excellent Bibliographies which the Institute has issued and for the translations which it has sponsored of seminal works in moral and political theory, such as John Locke’s Letters Concerning Toleration. Even more important have been his organization and editorship of the volumes of Chroniques in which experts on all the branches of philosophy have combined to give an illuminating overall picture of the contemporary state of the subject. I cannot think of anyone else
